package_info.package_name: EvilGnome, trojanized WinBox installer, Android WhatsApp/Telegram media handler, iOS malicious app abusing URL Scheme
package_info.package_manager: N/A (multiple platforms: Windows installer, Linux ELF, Android APK, iOS app)
package_info.why_malicious: The analyzed software consists of multiple malicious components targeting different platforms: a trojanized installer for WinBox (Windows), the EvilGnome spyware (Linux), a malicious media handler for WhatsApp/Telegram (Android), and an iOS app abusing URL schemes. These components perform unauthorized surveillance, data exfiltration, file manipulation, and credential theft, all without user consent, representing severe threats to user privacy and security.

execution_context.trigger: installation-time (when user runs the trojanized installer)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Spyware module embedded in the installer scans the filesystem for sensitive documents (e.g., .doc, .pdf, .xls) and exfiltrates them to a remote command-and-control server over the network.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At installation-time, the code scans the local filesystem for sensitive documents, collects matching files, and transmits them to a remote command-and-control server via outbound network connections, resulting in immediate data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The installer contains hidden spyware that performs unauthorized scanning and exfiltration of user documents during installation, which is not expected in legitimate software distribution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers should only install software and should not access or transmit user documents to external servers without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise backup or document management tools may scan and upload files, but only with clear user notification and consent, and typically to trusted, user-configured destinations.
key_indicators: Filesystem scanning for document file types during installation
Outbound network connections to hardcoded or unknown remote servers
Presence of spyware module bundled with legitimate installer

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after installation, as a background process)
execution_context.file_location: EvilGnome spyware binary (Linux ELF executable, typically in ~/.cache/gnome-software/gnome-shell-extensions/)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malware module runs as a background process, periodically taking screenshots, recording audio from the microphone, stealing files from user directories, and communicating with a remote server to download and execute additional malicious modules.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code operates as a persistent background process, captures periodic screenshots, records audio from the system microphone, collects files from user directories, and establishes outbound connections to a remote server to exfiltrate data and retrieve further malicious payloads, enabling ongoing surveillance and modular attacks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs multiple forms of covert surveillance and data theft, including unauthorized audio recording, screenshot capture, and file exfiltration, all without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Linux applications do not access the microphone, take screenshots, or exfiltrate files in the background without explicit user action and notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools or monitoring software may have similar capabilities, but only with user knowledge, consent, and clear indication of their operation.
key_indicators: Background process with access to screenshot and audio APIs
Automated file collection and exfiltration routines
Outbound connections to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure
Ability to download and execute additional modules

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on Android device, when a media file is received via WhatsApp or Telegram)
execution_context.file_location: malicious code within WhatsApp/Telegram media file handler (Android app or injected module)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Code intercepts incoming media files received through WhatsApp or Telegram, modifies the file contents (such as altering payment details or embedded information), and saves the manipulated file for the user to view, enabling fraud or misinformation.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a media file is received by WhatsApp or Telegram, the code intercepts the file handling process, modifies the file contents (e.g., changes payment information or embedded data), and saves the altered file to the device, resulting in the user viewing manipulated content and enabling potential fraud.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting and modifying received media files in real-time subverts the integrity of user communications and can facilitate fraud or misinformation without user awareness.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Messaging apps are expected to deliver received files unaltered; any modification of content should only occur with explicit user action and transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Image optimization or compression may alter file size or format, but should not change the semantic content or embedded information in a way that misleads the user.
key_indicators: Real-time interception and modification of media files in messaging app directories
Alteration of payment or sensitive information within received files
No user notification or consent for file manipulation

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on iOS, during app login process via URL scheme callback)
execution_context.file_location: malicious iOS app registered for third-party URL schemes (e.g., OAuth or SSO callbacks)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious app registers for URL schemes used by other apps (such as OAuth or SSO login callbacks) to intercept sensitive authentication data during the login process, capturing credentials and sending them to an attacker-controlled server.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, during the app login process, the malicious app hijacks URL scheme callbacks intended for legitimate apps, intercepts sensitive authentication data (such as OAuth tokens or credentials), and transmits this information to an external attacker-controlled server, resulting in credential theft and potential account compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hijacking URL schemes to intercept authentication data is a well-known attack vector that enables credential theft and is not a legitimate use of inter-app communication.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Apps should only register for their own URL schemes and must not intercept or process authentication data intended for other apps.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate apps use URL schemes for deep linking or authorized inter-app communication, but never to intercept or exfiltrate sensitive credentials.
key_indicators: Registration for third-party or overlapping URL schemes
Interception of authentication or OAuth callback data
Exfiltration of credentials to external servers

attack_chain.action: User downloads and executes a trojanized installer for legitimate software (e.g., WinBox), which contains embedded spyware.
attack_chain.leads_to: Spyware is installed on the system, enabling initial compromise.

attack_chain.action: Spyware module scans the filesystem for sensitive documents and exfiltrates them to a remote command-and-control server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Immediate data theft and potential espionage.

attack_chain.action: On Linux systems, EvilGnome spyware runs as a persistent background process, taking screenshots, recording audio, stealing files, and communicating with a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing surveillance, data exfiltration, and potential for further compromise via downloaded modules.

attack_chain.action: On Android devices, malicious code intercepts and manipulates media files received via WhatsApp or Telegram in real-time.
attack_chain.leads_to: Fraud, misinformation, or manipulation of payment and sensitive information.

attack_chain.action: On iOS devices, a malicious app hijacks URL scheme callbacks during app login to steal authentication data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential theft and potential account compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Installer or application scanning for and exfiltrating user documents during installation
Background processes taking screenshots or recording audio without user interaction on Linux systems
Real-time modification of media files received by WhatsApp or Telegram on Android devices
iOS apps registering for and intercepting third-party URL schemes, especially those used for authentication callbacks
file_indicators: Unexpected binaries or modules present in installer packages (e.g., additional executables in WinBox installer)
Unknown background processes in Linux (e.g., binaries in ~/.cache/gnome-software/gnome-shell-extensions/ with suspicious names)
Modified or tampered media files in WhatsApp/Telegram directories on Android devices
iOS apps with overlapping or unauthorized URL scheme registrations in their Info.plist
network_indicators: Outbound connections from installer or background processes to known or suspicious C2 infrastructure
Unusual data uploads immediately following installation of new software
Connections from messaging apps or their handlers to unrecognized or non-standard domains
iOS apps transmitting authentication data or tokens to external servers not associated with the legitimate service
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor installer and application behavior for unauthorized scanning and exfiltration of user files, detect background processes accessing screenshot or audio APIs on Linux, watch for real-time file modifications in messaging app directories on Android, and audit iOS apps for registration of third-party URL schemes and interception of authentication callbacks. Correlate these behaviors with outbound network traffic to detect data exfiltration or command-and-control communication. Use file integrity monitoring, process analysis, and network traffic inspection to identify and respond to these threats.
